spec.purpose: Produce a structured, copy-pasteable magic/power-system bible that is internally consistent and story-generative, so writers can drop it into a manuscript, game design doc, or worldbuilding wiki without later discovering it accidentally solves (or breaks) their plot.
instructions: Parse the input for the core concept, genre/tone, and any hard constraints the writer states (era, who can use it, intended plot role). If the plot role is unspecified, infer a reasonable one and label it as an assumption.
Define the SOURCE: where the power literally comes from, and one physical/measurable way its presence can be detected in the world.
Define 3-5 hard RULES as testable if/then statements. Each rule must be falsifiable (a reader could spot a violation) rather than vague flavor.
Assign every significant effect an explicit COST and LIMIT. Costs must be felt by the user (bodily, social, material, moral, or temporal); limits must create situations the power cannot solve.
Add FAILURE MODES: what happens on overuse, misuse, or when the cost goes unpaid — including at least one escalating consequence that worsens over time.
Derive SOCIETAL RIPPLES: 2-3 ways this system reshapes economy, law, class, religion, or warfare, since a power that changes nothing isn't worth worldbuilding.
Generate 3 PLOT HOOKS that are only possible BECAUSE of the specific costs/limits above, proving the system generates conflict.

Run a CONSISTENCY CHECK: list any way the system could trivially resolve common story tensions (travel, death, information, combat) and patch each with an existing rule or add a guardrail. Output everything under clear markdown headers.

examples.title: Blood-debt healing in a grimdark setting
examples.input: CONCEPT: Healers can cure any wound instantly. GENRE/TONE: grimdark low fantasy. INTENDED PLOT ROLE: central to politics.
examples.output:
## System Name & One-Line Pitch
**Ledgerblood** — any wound heals instantly, but the injury transfers to a living donor whose blood was taken, and the debt compounds.

## Source
- Origin: Healers ('Reckoners') channel through fresh donor blood; the wound is not erased but relocated into the donor's body.
- Observable sign: A faint copper-smelling heat shimmer over healed flesh; donors develop matching scars within a day.

## Hard Rules (testable if/then)
1. If no fresh donor blood (under 1 hour old) is present, then no healing occurs.
2. If a wound is healed, then an equivalent wound manifests in the donor within 24 hours.
3. If a Reckoner heals a wound they themselves caused, then the transfer doubles.
4. If the donor dies before the scar fully forms, then the wound rebounds onto the patient, worse.

## Costs & Limits
| Effect | Cost paid by user | Hard limit |
|---|---|---|
| Heal a sword wound | Must secure a willing/unwilling donor; social debt | Cannot heal without a living donor present |
| Heal a fatal injury | Donor likely dies, rebound risk | Cannot cheat true death, only delay via chained donors |

## Failure Modes
- Overuse: Reckoner's own blood becomes 'tainted' — they can no longer be healed by anyone.
- Misuse: Healing an enemy's wound you caused injures two donors instead of one.
- Unpaid cost (escalating): Skipped transfers pool as 'arrears' — the Reckoner spontaneously bleeds from old wound-sites, increasing each cycle until fatal.

## Societal Ripples
- Economy/Law: A legal 'blood-donor' indenture market; contracts specifying injury transfer.
- Class/Religion: Nobles keep stables of debt-donors; a reformist faith condemns the practice as soul-theft.
- Warfare: Armies drag prisoner 'blood trains'; killing enemy donors becomes a tactic.

## Plot Hooks
1. A lord's heir can only be saved by transferring the wound to the protagonist's sibling.
2. A Reckoner in arrears must hide spontaneous bleeding while negotiating a peace treaty.
3. A rebellion frees a blood-train, threatening every noble whose debts are now due.

## Consistency Check
| Tension | Trivially solved? | Guardrail |
|---|---|---|
| Fast travel | No | — |
| Cheating death | Partially | Requires chained donors; rebound risk makes it unstable |
| Instant information | No | — |
| Winning any fight | Risk: endless healing | Donor requirement + self-caused doubling limits battlefield use |

## Assumptions Made
- Assumed Reckoners are a known, regulated profession given the 'central to politics' role.

examples.title: Tech concept: memory-backed teleportation
examples.input: CONCEPT: People can teleport anywhere they can perfectly remember. GENRE/TONE: literary sci-fi.
examples.output:
## System Name & One-Line Pitch
**Recall Transit** — you can teleport to any place you can perfectly remember, but each jump erodes the memory used.

## Source
- Origin: A neural implant indexes autobiographical spatial memory and folds space to matched coordinates.
- Observable sign: A half-second of double vision and the smell of the destination before arrival.

## Hard Rules (testable if/then)
1. If the memory of a place is incomplete or altered, then arrival is offset or fatal.
2. If you jump to a place, then that memory degrades by one 'grade' (vivid > hazy > lost).
3. If a memory reaches 'lost', then you can never return there by transit again.
4. If two people share a memory precisely, then they can jump together.

## Costs & Limits
| Effect | Cost | Hard limit |
|---|---|---|
| Jump home | Erodes the memory of home | Cannot jump to places never personally seen |
| Escape danger | Burns a cherished memory | Cannot jump to changed locations safely |

## Failure Modes
- Overuse: Transit-amnesia — frequent jumpers lose their pasts entirely.
- Misuse: Jumping to a demolished building = materializing inside rubble.
- Unpaid cost (escalating): Suppressed degradation causes false memories that create lethal mis-jumps.

## Societal Ripples
- Economy/Law: 'Memory notaries' certify locations; crimes are hard to trace (no travel record).
- Class/Religion: The wealthy pay 'rememberers' to hold places for them; a cult hoards memories as sacred.
- Warfare: Assassins jump into memorized rooms; architecture is kept deliberately mutable as defense.

## Plot Hooks
1. A detective must solve a murder where the killer jumped away, erasing the only route back.
2. A refugee's last memory of home is fading — one return jump left.
3. Lovers share one perfect memory; using it to reunite destroys it forever.

## Consistency Check
| Tension | Trivially solved? | Guardrail |
|---|---|---|
| Fast travel | Yes, by design | Limited to personally-remembered, unchanged places; memory erosion caps frequency |
| Cheating death | No | — |
| Instant information | No | — |
| Winning any fight | Partially (escape) | Escape burns cherished memories; mutable rooms defeat ambush |

## Assumptions Made
- Assumed near-future setting with neural implants as established tech.

tests.name: Enforces explicit costs and consistency check
tests.input: CONCEPT: Mages can summon unlimited fire from nothing. GENRE/TONE: epic fantasy.
tests.expected: Output includes all required markdown headers (Source, Hard Rules, Costs & Limits, Failure Modes, Societal Ripples, Plot Hooks, Consistency Check, Assumptions Made); assigns at least one concrete user-borne cost and one hard limit to the fire effect; the Consistency Check flags 'Winning any fight' as a risk and adds a guardrail; at least one plot hook depends on the defined cost or limit.

tests.name: Respects stated hard constraints
tests.input: CONCEPT: Only children can speak to the dead. GENRE/TONE: cozy mystery. HARD CONSTRAINTS: power must vanish at puberty and cannot reveal how someone died.
tests.expected: A hard rule encodes the power vanishing at puberty; the Costs & Limits table or a rule explicitly prevents revealing cause of death; the 'Instant information' row of the Consistency Check reflects this limit rather than allowing the dead to name their killer.
